The first time I saw the ocean, I was six years old. My family had driven for hours to reach the coast, and when we finally stepped onto the warm sand, I froze. The water stretched endlessly, shimmering under the sun, and the waves crashed with a sound like thunder. I remember clutching my father’s hand, half in awe, half in fear. He laughed and said, *"It’s just water, kid. It won’t bite."*

But the ocean did bite—just not in the way I expected. It taught me that beauty and danger often walk hand in hand. The waves could be gentle, lulling you into a false sense of safety before suddenly pulling you under. The tides were unpredictable, shifting without warning. And yet, there was something mesmerizing about it—the way the horizon blurred the line between sky and sea, the way the salt in the air made everything feel alive.

Years later, I still return to the ocean whenever I need to remember that life isn’t meant to be controlled. It’s meant to be felt—every crash, every calm, every unexpected storm. The ocean doesn’t ask for permission to change; it simply does. And in that relentless rhythm, there’s a strange kind of peace.

Maybe that’s why I love it. It’s a reminder that some things are too vast to fully understand, too powerful to resist. All you can do is stand at the shore, let the waves wash over your feet, and accept the mystery.
